cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the thoughts are coming into line.
cells.ask: When three things are up for deciding, say what a fair outcome looks like before any call gets made, and let it shape the call. Notice whether fairness got simpler once you stopped weighing it.
cells.core:
There's a lot up in the air, and you're the one getting it into order. Not forcing it — sorting it, so the people standing in the mess can walk through. That's the work, and it's happening now.

What's running under it is fairness you don't calculate. You can feel what's owed and to whom without running a ledger, and it holds when you say no. That's what's balanced here: you can give and receive, and neither throws it off. Keep this small — before a decision, name what fair looks like, and let that hold the line. It keeps the ordering yours instead of just clean.
cells.sheetLine: You can sort it, and you can stay fair while you do.

cells.tense: You are already standing in how it will have to go, before anyone has said anything.
cells.ask: Take the one conversation you keep rehearsing and set it down for today. Walk in without the plan. Whatever gets decided from there, decide it there.
cells.core:
You can see how the pieces should fit. So you're already building the structure ahead of time — for the talk that hasn't happened, for the way people will have to be arranged. You're doing tomorrow's tidying tonight, and it buys you very little.

What's steering is the plan, not the moment. You want to move from what's actually in front of you, not from the diagram you drew of it. So set down the one thing you keep running. Walk in without it. If the plan really matters, it'll still be available then, with better information. What's lost is only the pre-loading.
cells.sheetLine: You've already built it. Nobody asked you to build it yet.

cells.tense: You used to be the one who sorted it, and you haven't come back through that door.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you feel about how matters stand between you, no resolution required and no plan attached. Then let them answer.
cells.core:
You are not the one holding the arrangement anymore. Things happen and you let them, and the structure you used to keep isn't being kept. It's not laziness. You pulled your weight out of it, and it has been drifting since.

What's missing is the feel for who owes what to whom. That doesn't come back by reasoning; it refills by being with someone and letting what you actually feel about the situation show. So say one true thing to one person about how things stand. Not to fix anything — to let the connection carry some of it. Small and honest is enough. The structure comes back after the contact, not before.
cells.sheetLine: You stepped out of the arranging. Let someone in before you step back in.

cells.tense: The structure is holding, and you keep calling it everyone's arrangement but yours.
cells.ask: Say out loud once, one way you shaped how things run — not what you're responsible for, but what you made. Then notice whether you still call it an accident.
cells.core:
Things around you have a shape: how decisions get made, what people expect, what happens when there's a snag. You built a lot of that. But when you describe it you say it's just how things are, or how the group runs, as if the pattern assembled itself.

It didn't. You've been setting the tone and the rules and the way the work gets divided, and doing it well enough that it looks automatic. That's what makes it communal, and it's also why nobody marks it yours. The pattern wasn't just handed down; you taught it by doing it and letting others do it too. Naming one piece as yours costs nothing and returns the credit to where it belongs. Nothing about the arrangement has to change for that to be true.
cells.sheetLine: You built the pattern. You're calling it how things just are.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that these people have a felt moral compass running under the gathering of thoughts — the record says it is the medicine, not the state, so I must write fair exchange as the invitation and never assert they already feel it. A reader could reasonably say the sorting is just being tired or busy, not a pattern; the asks still work if I am wrong because each one only asks for a next physical step, not a feeling. The sentence that serves me more than them is the tidy phrase 'gathering your own harvest' — it flatters the writer and says nothing a person could do.
